title: Spec section 4.3 promises the framework's own diagnostic on stderr, but the send_error override means log_error is never called at all
finding: Section 4.3 states that log_error still writes the framework's own message, including the offending token, to stderr, and calls it the owner's diagnostic. That is not what happens. log_error is invoked only from BaseHTTPRequestHandler.send_error; because send_error is overridden here (server.py:357-359) and goes straight to _respond_plain, log_error is never reached. I instrumented Handler.log_error and drove a 505, a 501 and a 400 over raw sockets: 0 invocations. The spec sentence therefore describes behaviour that the design it also mandates makes impossible - a plan defect rather than a build defect, since the override is exactly what sections 4.3 and 4.3.1 require. Impact is small, and was reduced further by the CR-005-11 fix: log_request now writes a line of the form 'server: 127.0.0.1 - <repr of the request line> <status> -' for every refusal, so the owner still gets the request line (which carries the offending method token or version) and the status code. What is lost is CPython's explanatory wording, for example 'Invalid HTTP version (2.5)'; and on the 414 path the request line has already been blanked to the empty string by handle_one_request, so a 414 logs only that it happened. PBI-007 captures this stderr to the owner's log file, which is the consumer that cares. The builder found and disclosed this itself (change-report-r2, follow-up 3); it was not in the round-1 findings and it is not a regression - it has been true since round 1.
remediation: The owner's call, and cheapest as a spec edit rather than a code change: at the next revision of docs/backlog/specs/pbi-005-local-server.md, reword section 4.3's log_error sentence to say that the overridden send_error emits the diagnostic through log_request (the repr-escaped request line plus the status) and that CPython's own explanatory message is deliberately not kept. If the wording is wanted instead, the override can call self.log_error before _respond_plain - but that would put framework text on stderr that the CR-005-11 escaping does not cover, so the spec edit is the better option. Non-blocking.

title: Section 6.3's rule that any unexpected exception in a handler returns 500 is not honoured for an OSError, and the new test now pins the no-response behaviour as the contract
finding: The except OSError clause in _handle (server.py:369-374) sits above except Exception, so an OSError raised anywhere inside routing - not only a broken pipe - is logged and swallowed with no response written. Section 6.3's table says any unexpected exception in a handler yields 500 with the line 'the server failed to handle this request'. The new test Errors.test_an_os_error_inside_a_handler_is_named_on_stderr (test_server.py:606-615) asserts that the raw response is empty, which turns 'no response at all' from an accident into a pinned contract. This is explicitly one of the two remediations my own round-1 CR-005-03 offered (keep a single except OSError here but emit one warn line naming the errno before passing), and the observability half I actually raised is genuinely fixed: I mutated server.warn to drop that line and the test fails with 'errno 13 not found in'. So this is recorded for completeness, not as a re-raise and not as a moved goalpost. In practice the clause is almost always right: the only OSErrors reachable in that block are socket writes from _serve_page and _serve_snapshot, which have no try of their own, and for those a dropped connection is the correct answer because the peer has gone. A genuine non-connection OSError (a file-descriptor or disk fault) is the case where a 500 would be better than a silent close, and the owner now at least gets the errno on stderr.
remediation: Either narrow the clause to the connection-loss errnos (EPIPE, ECONNRESET, ECONNABORTED, ETIMEDOUT and the WSAE equivalents on Windows) and let except Exception answer 500 for the rest, or leave the code as it is and add a sentence to section 6.3 saying an OSError is treated as connection loss and answered with a close plus one stderr line rather than a 500. Either way, loosen the test so it pins the stderr line rather than the absence of a response. Non-blocking; a later pass.

title: The HTTP/0.9 version forcing is applied only in _respond_plain, not in the three success writers - unreachable on the shipped interpreter, recorded so it is not lost
finding: This is the assessment of the builder's new, previously unreviewed defect fix, and the fix is correct. I verified CPython 3.14.5's parse_request: self.request_version is assigned only after the 505 and bad-version-400 checks, so it is still HTTP/0.9 when send_error runs, and send_response_only, send_header and end_headers all gate on request_version differing from HTTP/0.9 and emit nothing. _respond_plain (server.py:440-441) now forces the version, and over raw sockets all six framework-raised paths - 400 (malformed line), 400 (bad version), 414, 431, 501 and 505 - come back with a correct status line and 9 headers: Content-Type text/plain; charset=utf-8, Cache-Control no-store, nosniff, a Content-Length equal to the body, and Connection: close. The connection still closes, because send_header sets close_connection outside the version gate, so nothing is left half-open. The status line uses protocol_version, not the client's claimed version, so nothing new is echoed: I swept a marker token through the Host, Origin, method, request line, version and a header name, and found it in neither the body nor the headers of any of eight responses. Mutating the forcing back to a no-op makes GateFramework.test_every_refusal_has_the_same_plain_shape fail, so the fix is pinned by a test that bites. On the builder's own question - whether a genuine HTTP/0.9 client now receives headers it does not understand - the answer on this interpreter is better than it feared: CPython 3.14 sets self.headers to an empty dict and returns immediately for a two-word request line, on the stated grounds that HTTP/0.9 expects no headers at all. Such a request therefore carries no Host header, is refused 403 by the gate, and can never reach a route. I confirmed that empirically: GET / and GET /api/snapshot over HTTP/0.9, even with a Host header supplied, both return 403 and no board data. The trade is acceptable, and AC-SV2's uniform shape is the right thing to optimise for on a server that binds 127.0.0.1 and serves a browser. The only residue is an asymmetry: the forcing lives in _respond_plain but not in _serve_page, _serve_snapshot or _serve_events. On CPython 3.14 that is unreachable. On an older supported interpreter (the suite's stated floor is 3.11) whose HTTP/0.9 branch parsed headers, a local process could pass the gate over HTTP/0.9 and receive a 200 whose status line, Content-Type, nosniff and CSP were all suppressed. I had no 3.11 interpreter to test here, so this is a bounded risk, not a measured defect; either way it needs a process already running on the machine, which can read the database file directly, so there is no privilege gain.
remediation: No change required for merge. If it is wanted for tidiness and for older interpreters, hoist the two-line version check out of _respond_plain into a small helper called at the top of _respond_plain, _serve_page, _serve_snapshot and _serve_events, so one rule covers every response this module writes. Worth one sentence in section 4.3 recording why the version is forced at all.

title: Leftover unused state in the live-test fixture
finding: Live.setUp captures both server.POLL_DEFAULT and server.HEARTBEAT, into self._orig_poll and self._orig_heartbeat. Only _orig_heartbeat is used (line 23 restores it through addCleanup); _orig_poll is never read, and POLL_DEFAULT is never patched by this class - the poll interval is passed per server through start(poll=...). It reads as if a module constant were being saved for restoration when it is not, which is the kind of half-removed scaffolding that later misleads someone into thinking POLL_DEFAULT is mutated somewhere. Catalogue rule: Dead Code and Leftover State.
